knowledge_point.title: Finding General Solutions by Rearranging Then Integrating

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y'+11y=0$ for $y\ne0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y'+11y=0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+11y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-11y \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-11)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (-11)\,\text{d}x \\ \ln|y| & =- 11 x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln|y|=- 11 x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln|y| & =- 11 x+C \\ |y| & =e^{- 11 x+C} \\ |y| & =e^{- 11 x}\cdot e^C \\ |y| & =K e^{- 11 x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=e^C$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K e^{- 11 x}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y'-6 xy=0$ for $y\ne0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y'-6 xy=0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6 xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (6 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \ln|y| & =3 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\ln|y|=3 x^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln|y| & =3 x^{2}+C \\ |y| & =e^{3 x^{2}+C} \\ |y| & =e^{3 x^{2}}\cdot e^C \\ |y| & =K e^{3 x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=e^C$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K e^{3 x^{2}}.
$$
